title: Move DIV/REM off EX critical path
motivation:
The baseline timing path runs from MEM/WB forwarding control through the EX
operand muxes into the ALU and reaches about 150 logic levels. The current
ALU contains fully combinational RV32M divide and remainder operators, so even
ordinary forwarded ADD/load-address operations share timing with the largest
arithmetic cone. Removing the divider from the single-cycle EX path should
raise Fmax by far more than the acceptance threshold, while CoreMark is
expected to execute few or no DIV/REM instructions in the measured loop.

hypothesis.hypothesis:
Replace the combinational DIV/DIVU/REM/REMU logic in the ALU with a small
iterative divider/remainder unit that stalls the in-order pipeline only while
one of those rare operations is in EX. Keep ADD/SUB/logic/shift/compare and
DSP-backed MUL/MULH operations single-cycle, and have EX/MEM capture the
DIV/REM result only on the unit's done pulse. This should cut the current
ALU-forwarding critical path while preserving exact RV32M results and RVFI
retirement order.

title: Split RV32M off the EX fast path
motivation:
The baseline timing report points through the forwarding muxes into EX and
then through the monolithic combinational ALU. That ALU contains full 32-bit
multiply, divide, and remainder operators even though ordinary RV32I ALU,
branch, and address-generation operations dominate CoreMark cycles. The
current structure pays the RV32M timing cost on every instruction.

title: Static loop branch predictor
motivation:
The current five-stage pipeline fetches linearly and redirects only after EX
resolves a taken branch or jump. CoreMark has many loop backedges, so the core
repeatedly pays taken-branch flush bubbles even though those branches are easy
to predict from their immediate direction. The existing critical path is in the
EX ALU/forwarding logic, so a very small IF-side predictor has a chance to
improve iterations per cycle without materially changing Fmax.

title: Decouple fetch flush from hazard decode
motivation:
After the iterative DIV/REM change, the measured worst path no longer runs
through the divider; it runs through the ID, EX redirect, IF flush, hazard,
and ID/EX capture-control cone. The current IF stage rewrites fetched
instruction bits to a NOP on flush so the hazard unit sees harmless register
numbers. That makes a control decision from EX feed back through IF into
load-use detection and then into the ID/EX register mux, which is exactly the
new timing bottleneck.

title: Tiny trained branch target predictor
motivation:
The current core still resolves all taken branches and jumps in EX, so loop
backedges in CoreMark inject redirect bubbles even though the same PCs repeat
many times. The previous static predictor showed that removing those bubbles
can reduce CoreMark cycles, but it put immediate decode and target arithmetic
directly on the IF next-PC path and destroyed Fmax. A predictor that learns
resolved targets and reuses registered targets should keep the timing cost
much lower.

motivation:

title: Add a one-entry store drain buffer
motivation:
The current best core is no longer dominated by the old RV32M divider path;
its Fmax is around 52 MHz and CoreMark still runs under the benchmark's
realistic pseudo-random dmem backpressure. Today any store sitting in MEM
freezes IF, ID, and EX until io_dmemReady returns, even though later integer
work usually does not need the store to have physically drained. A small
structural decoupling point can attack measured cycles without adding a
predictor or another global front-end stage, both of which have recently
hurt this design.

hypothesis.hypothesis:

Ordinary stores retire into the buffer when the bus is stalled, and the

useful fraction of the 22% random dStall cost for CoreMark stores with much
less Fmax risk than front-end prediction or a full pipeline-depth change.

title: Return-address stack predictor
motivation:
The prior predictor experiments proved that CoreMark has enough taken-control
bubbles to matter, but both broad predictors hurt Fmax by putting branch
target calculation or BTB/BHT lookup logic directly on the IF next-PC path.
A return predictor is a narrower control-flow predictor with a much cheaper
fetch-side decision: exact RET instruction detection plus a registered stack
target, with no immediate adder, tag RAM, or saturating counter lookup.

still injects a full bubble for every adjacent load-use pair even when the
combinational dmem returns data in the same MEM cycle. Prior structural
attempts that deepened execute or buffered fetch improved one side of the
score while losing the other. A load-specific bypass attacks cycles within

title: ID-registered target prefetch predictor
motivation:
The strongest predictor attempts so far were the resolved redirect-folding
variants: they cut CoreMark cycles by fetching taken targets earlier, but
missed acceptance because EX redirect, imem address selection, and IF/ID
valid/flush gating stayed on a critical front-end feedback path. Earlier
IF-time BTB, BHT, RAS, and static immediate predictors were worse because
target lookup or immediate arithmetic sat directly on the normal PC path.

normal sequential fetch path. Keeping the prediction metadata in a small

title: Qualify load-use source operands
motivation:
The current core still pays a one-cycle load-use interlock whenever a load's
destination register matches either raw source field of the following
instruction. That is conservative but over-stalls for OP-IMM, LOAD, JALR,
LUI, AUIPC, JAL, FENCE, SYSTEM, and many illegal encodings where instr[24:20]
or instr[19:15] is not an architecturally consumed operand. Recent attempts
that added EX bypass inputs or front-end speculation widened timing cones, so
a narrow hazard-only IPC cleanup is the best remaining micro-opt angle.

title: Unified-PC split execute
motivation:
The best structural result so far was the simple EX0/EX1 split: it raised
median Fmax to about 63 MHz, but lost too many CoreMark cycles from added
branch and dependency latency. Later attempts to recover those cycles either
over-stalled or broke the RVFI pc_fwd contract by letting early and late
redirect paths disagree about the retiring instruction's pc_wdata.

That makes the most promising structural target a corrected version of the
split-execute idea, not another fetch queue, store buffer, or predictor path.

motivation:
Prior predictor attempts show that CoreMark can benefit from removing taken
direct-branch bubbles, but the implementations that confirmed prediction in
the same cycle as EX resolution lost too much Fmax through redirect, imem,
and IF/ID flush gating. The best near-miss reduced cycles enough to almost
clear the tournament threshold, so the promising angle is to keep the target
fetch benefit while taking EX branch confirmation out of the target-accept
timing path.

hypothesis.hypothesis:
Add a tiny branch-target instruction cache for direct JAL and conditional branch targets, but precheck it before the redirect cycle. When a direct control-flow instruction enters ID/EX, use its PC and ID-computed pc+imm target to look up a one- or two-entry BTIC and latch hit plus cached target instruction in a narrow sideband aligned with EX. title: Narrow pipeline bubble clears
motivation: The current best designs are limited by the register-file/ID-to-EX ALU result cone, and recent attempts that added new prediction or forwarding sideband widened that same path.  Several stage registers still clear whole packed structs on reset, flush, invalid fetch, or DIV/REM busy bubbles even though the datapath fields are ignored whenever valid is low.  Those zero arms become extra mux inputs on hot operand and EX/MEM result flops without improving CoreMark IPC or correctness.

title: Stall-fill fetch skid buffer
motivation:
The current best core still pays independent random instruction-memory stalls
after cycles where the pipeline was already frozen by dmem backpressure or a
long EX operation. Prior full IF queues and predictors lost because they put
counters, target muxes, or prediction metadata on the normal fetch/decode
path. A narrower structure can exploit the same stalled-PC situation without
changing the fall-through PC path or speculating ahead.

hypothesis.hypothesis:
Add a one-entry fetch skid buffer that only fills while the PC is held for a

the buffered instruction for the held PC is supplied to ID even if the next

overlapping a fraction of the 22 percent imem stalls with dmem stalls while
adding only a small same-PC instruction/valid mux, not a predictor or queue
counter on the critical PC feedback path.

title: Flush-free direct fold sideband
motivation:
The best predictor attempts are the resolved-target redirect-fold designs:
they reduced CoreMark cycles from roughly 4.49M to about 4.15M, and the
registered direct-target fold reached 126.77 fitness, just below the
replacement threshold. Its timing miss was not the target add itself; Gowin
reported a long redirect/imem-ready/flush cone feeding the wide ID-stage
direct_target register. That suggests the remaining opportunity is to keep
the same conservative direct-control fold while removing fold acceptance from
wide payload update logic.

and back into ID's wide direct_target flop. JALR, misaligned targets,
imem-not-ready cycles, dmem stalls, and DIV/REM holds all remain on the
existing conservative redirect path, so correctness and RVFI PC sequencing
stay simple.

title: Replicate GPR read banks
motivation:
The current champion's worst path still launches from the register file and
runs through the ID/EX operand path, EX forwarding, and the ALU/load-address
cone.  Prior LUTRAM inference made this path slower, suggesting the problem
is not reset fanout but the hot asynchronous read/write-first mux structure.
The design has ample FF/LUT headroom, so spending area to reduce register-file
read fanout is a plausible Fmax win without changing CoreMark cycles.

title: Early MEM-stage writeback
motivation: The current best core is again limited by the register-file/read-to-EX ALU cone, with the reported path passing through ID, EX operand selection, the ALU, and EX/MEM capture. Prior predictor and fetch-buffer attempts mostly lost by widening front-end feedback, while split-EX attempts paid too much IPC and bypass-control cost. A narrower structural change should attack the execute operand mux directly without adding branch speculation or another execute stage.

hypothesis.hypothesis:
Move architectural register writes from the MEM/WB stage to an early MEM-stage write port, while keeping MEM/WB as the RVFI retirement boundary. For ALU/JAL/AUIPC/LUI results, the value in EX/MEM can drive the regfile write/bypass during the MEM cycle; for loads, the dmem read data can write only when the memory access is actually ready and not misaligned. With same-cycle write-first behavior in the regfile, instructions that are two cycles behind a producer capture the value in ID, so EX no longer needs the MEM/WB forwarding source.

The execute operand mux can then shrink from a three-source mux to a two-source mux: ID/EX register value or adjacent EX/MEM bypass. This should shorten the hot RF/ID-to-ALU path and remove MEM/WB write-data fanout from the forwarding network. The load-use interlock remains for adjacent loads, dmem stalls still hold the pipeline until a load/store is accepted, and traps or x0 writes suppress the early write, so RVFI order and architectural correctness stay unchanged even though the physical regfile updates one cycle before the instruction's RVFI retirement pulse.

title: Verified return fold sideband
motivation:
The current champion made predictor-category progress only after avoiding the normal IF next-PC predictor path: direct branch and JAL targets are computed as a narrow ID sideband, then verified in EX and folded into fetch only on a resolved taken redirect.  That preserves the CoreMark cycle win while keeping the critical path near the existing register-file-to-ALU cone.

The remaining direct-control gap is JALR, especially function returns.  CoreMark still pays the ordinary redirect bubble for returns because their target depends on rs1, but a small return-address sideband can supply the likely target without putting instruction decode, a RAS mux, or a target adder on the speculative IF PC path.
